name: Weber syndrome
vascularTerritory: Paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery (posterior thalamoperforating / midbrain perforators)
presentation: Ipsilateral pupil-involving CN III palsy — ptosis, mydriasis, and a 'down and out' eye — combined with contralateral hemiplegia of face, arm, and leg and contralateral upper motor neuron facial weakness (crossed findings).
cause: Infarction or hemorrhage of the ventral midbrain at the basis pedunculi, damaging the oculomotor fascicles as they traverse the substance of the midbrain and the corticospinal/corticobulbar fibers of the crus cerebri; classically from occlusion of paramedian PCA perforators, also reported with tumors, demyelination, and tuberculoma.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126
Patten, Neurological Differential Diagnosis — midbrain level plates

name: Benedikt syndrome
vascularTerritory: Paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery (posterior thalamoperforating / paramedian midbrain)
presentation: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral involuntary movements — rubral tremor, choreoathetosis, or hemiataxia — plus contralateral impairment of touch, vibration, and position sense when the medial lemniscus is involved.
cause: Ventral tegmental lesion involving the CN III fascicles and the red nucleus / dentatorubrothalamic fibers with (variable) medial lemniscus extension; classically paramedian PCA perforator infarction, historically also tuberculosis and tumor.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Claude syndrome
vascularTerritory: Paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery
presentation: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with pronounced contralateral cerebellar ataxia — dysmetria, intention tremor, and incoordination — typically out of proportion to any weakness.
cause: Dorsal tegmental infarct in the paramedian PCA territory damaging the CN III fascicles together with the red nucleus and the dentatorubrothalamic (superior cerebellar peduncle) outflow; the ataxia reflects interruption of cerebellar output before its decussation.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Nothnagel syndrome
vascularTerritory: Superior cerebellar artery and collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the posterior cerebral artery
presentation: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia; vertical gaze palsy and other dorsal midbrain (tectal) signs may accompany the syndrome when the superior colliculus and pretectal region are involved.
cause: Lesion of the dorsal midbrain tectum and tegmentum — classically a quadrigeminal-plate tumor (pineal region) or an infarct in the SCA/PCA collicular territory — involving the CN III nucleus or fascicles, the superior colliculus, and the red nucleus.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain)
vascularTerritory: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the posterior cerebral artery; pineal region masses cause the syndrome by mass effect rather than ischemia
presentation: Vertical gaze palsy (upgaze affected first, later downgaze), convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, eyelid retraction (Collier sign), light-near dissociation with large pupils that accommodate but do not react to light, and the setting-sun sign.
cause: Compression or destruction of the dorsal midbrain and pretectal region: pineal region tumors, hydrocephalus with dilatation of the suprapineal recess, midbrain infarction (collicular/quadrigeminal branches), demyelination, or upper brainstem hemorrhage.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control" (supranuclear control of eye movements)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF)
vascularTerritory: Paramedian branches of the basilar artery
presentation: On attempted lateral gaze: impaired (slow or absent) adduction of the ipsilateral eye with abducting nystagmus of the contralateral eye; convergence is characteristically spared, distinguishing the lesion from a third-nerve palsy; diplopia occurs in lateral gaze.
cause: Lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus interrupting the abducens internuclear fibers that ascend to the contralateral oculomotor medial rectus subnucleus; in young adults usually demyelination (often bilateral), in the elderly a small paramedian basilar perforator infarct (usually unilateral).
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Parkinson's disease
presentation: Asymmetric resting 'pill-rolling' tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability; later autonomic dysfunction, REM-sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, and cognitive decline. Levodopa-responsive historically.
cause: Progressive degeneration of the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta with alpha-synuclein (Lewy body) inclusions; striatal dopamine depletion unbalances basal ganglia circuitry — reduced direct-pathway facilitation with relatively increased GABAergic output of the SNr/GPi onto thalamus and superior colliculus.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Basal Ganglia" (Parkinson's disease and related disorders)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Snell, Clinical Neuroanatomy — basal ganglia sections

name: Peduncular hallucinosis
vascularTerritory: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery (midbrain perforators and paramedian thalamic perforators, including artery-of-Percheron territory)
presentation: Vivid, colorful, complex visual hallucinations — people, animals, and scenes — with preserved insight and otherwise intact mental status, often worse in the evening or low light and frequently accompanied by sleep-wake disturbance; hallucinations are typically welcomed rather than threatening.
cause: Lesions of the rostral midbrain (cerebral peduncle, substantia nigra, red nucleus region) or the paramedian thalamus that disconnect ascending reticular and limbic visual circuitry from occipital association cortex; classically paramedian perforator infarcts, described by Lhermitte in 1922.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126
